nodes.content:
1950s to 1970s

Core Structure:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Large reduced-form systems of \textcolor{red}{aggregate variables} estimated on \textcolor{red}{historical time-series}. 
\end{itemize}\\

Critiques: 
Terrible performance in 1970s:
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Failed to forecast \textcolor{red}{stagflation} (stagnation and inflation).
        \item Subject to influential critiques by leading macroeconomists, including Lucas (1976): \noindent One of the most important \textcolor{red}{paradigm shifts} in modern \textcolor{red}{macroeconomic theory}. Policy evaluation cannot rely on non-\textcolor{red}{structural} relationships estimated from historical data, since parameters are not \textcolor{red}{invariant to policy}. Agents reoptimize and change their behaviour when policy changes. Models must instead be \textcolor{red}{micro-founded}: built on deep \textcolor{red}{primitive parameters} (preferences, technology, constraints) that are plausibly \textcolor{red}{invariant to policy}.
    \end{itemize}

nodes.title: 1.1.6 Business Cycle Models: RBC, NK DSGE, HANK
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Models of the Business Cycle}}

{\footnotesize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.35}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.22\textwidth}|p{0.22\textwidth}|p{0.22\textwidth}|p{0.22\textwidth}@{}}
\hline
\textbf{RBC} & \textbf{NK} & \textbf{NK DSGE} & \textbf{HANK} \\
\hline\hline

\multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\textbf{Strengths}} \\
\hline

\textcolor{red}{Micro-founded}, optimization-based, intertemporal. Built on \textcolor{red}{deep parameters} (preferences, technology, constraints). Ok performance on aggregate comovement. Addressed the \textcolor{red}{Lucas critique}. &

Accounts for: (1) \textcolor{red}{nominal rigidities} and \textcolor{red}{monetary non-neutrality}, (2) other frictions (labor market, financial). &

NK $+$ RBC: \textcolor{red}{DSGE framework} $+$ \textcolor{red}{imperfect competition} $+$ \textcolor{red}{nominal rigidities}. Richer shocks (demand, cost-push, policy). Role for \textcolor{red}{stabilization policy}. Microfounds Keynesian concepts. &

NK DSGE $+$ \textcolor{red}{heterogeneous agents}: idiosyncratic income risk, imperfect insurance, heterogeneous MPCs. Micro $\to$ macro: new transmission channels. Macro $\to$ micro: new distributional effects. \\
\hline

\multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\textbf{Weaknesses}} \\
\hline

(1) Representative agent. (2) No frictions/rigidities. (3) Mainly technology shocks. \newline
\textit{Consequences:} (i) too little volatility in hours, (ii) weak internal propagation, (iii) fluctuations efficient $\Rightarrow$ no role for stabilization policy. \newline
\textbf{But:} Volcker disinflation proves monetary policy has real effects $+$ micro evidence on price stickiness $+$ countercyclical labor wedge $=$ \textcolor{red}{inefficient labor fluctuations exist}. &

Largely \textcolor{red}{static}. Mainly \textcolor{red}{qualitative}. &

\textcolor{red}{Representative agent}: no distributional effects.$^*$ &

Computational complexity. Open: endogenous unemployment risk, optimal policy, firm heterogeneity, network interactions. \\
\hline

\multicolumn{4}{@{}l@{}}{\textbf{Evaluation}} \\
\hline

Pioneered \textcolor{red}{calibration}: compare data vs model moments (std devs, autocorrelations, cross-correlations --- the ``KP table''). \textit{Refer to calibration note.} & & & \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
}

\medskip
{\footnotesize $^*$\textbf{But when should we introduce heterogeneity?}

\textcolor{red}{Macro $\to$ micro}: what are the distributional effects of shocks/policy? (e.g.\ does expansionary monetary policy benefit poorer HHs more?) A model can only answer this if it explicitly incorporates heterogeneity.

\textcolor{red}{Micro $\to$ macro}: do distributional features affect aggregate transmission? (e.g.\ do liquidity-constrained HHs alter the aggregate response?) This is a quantitative question --- sometimes a representative-agent model suffices.

\textit{This has vast consequences for optimal monetary and fiscal policy.}

\medskip
\textbf{Case study: the Great Recession.} The GR originated in housing/credit markets. Falling house prices had \textcolor{red}{heterogeneous effects} depending on balance-sheet composition. Pass-through to consumption varied with \textcolor{red}{liquidity} and \textcolor{red}{MPCs}. Demand collapse generated \textcolor{red}{uneven employment losses} across occupations and skill groups. Representative-agent models couldn't capture these channels.
}

nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Euler Equation via Envelope Theorem (Planner)}}

{\footnotesize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.6}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.94\textwidth}@{}}
\hline
\textbf{Step 0 --- States and controls} \\
\hline
\textbf{States:} $k$ (endogenous), $\textcolor{red}{A, s}$ (exogenous). \textbf{Controls:} $\textcolor{blue}{n}, k'$ (not $c$: substituted out in Step 1). \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 1 --- Substitute $c$ out, define $\Phi$} \\
\hline
Constraint binds (Inada). Replace $c = \textcolor{red}{A}F(k,\textcolor{blue}{n}) + (1{-}\delta)k - k'$: \\[3pt]
$\Phi(k,\textcolor{blue}{n},k') = u\!\big(\underbrace{\textcolor{red}{A}F(k,\textcolor{blue}{n}) + (1{-}\delta)k - k'}_{= \, c},\; \textcolor{blue}{n}\big) + \beta\,\textcolor{red}{\mathbb{E}[V(k', A', s') \mid s]}$ \\[3pt]
\textit{From now on, $u_c$ means $\partial u/\partial c$ (derivative w.r.t.\ consumption), not w.r.t.\ the long expression inside $u$. We write $u_c$ because we already substituted $c$ out --- the chain rule handles the rest.} \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 2 --- FOC w.r.t.\ each control} \\
\hline
\textbf{$[\textcolor{blue}{n}]$:} $u_c \cdot \textcolor{red}{A}F_n + u_n = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{-u_n = u_c \cdot \textcolor{red}{A}F_n}$ \quad\textit{(intratemporal)} \\[6pt]
\textbf{$[k']$:} $u_c \cdot (-1) + \beta\,\textcolor{red}{\mathbb{E}[V_k(k', A', s') \mid s]} = 0$ \quad\textit{($V_k$ is abstract --- need Steps 3--4)} \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 3 --- Envelope: differentiate $V$ w.r.t.\ endogenous state $k$} \\
\hline
$V_k = \underbrace{\partial\Phi/\partial k}_{\text{direct}} + \underbrace{\partial\Phi/\partial \textcolor{blue}{n}}_{=\,0\;\text{(FOC)}} \cdot N'_k + \underbrace{\partial\Phi/\partial k'}_{=\,0\;\text{(FOC)}} \cdot G'_k$ \\[3pt]
Control terms vanish (envelope theorem). Only direct effect survives: \\[3pt]
$\boxed{V_k(k, \textcolor{red}{A, s}) = u_c \cdot [\textcolor{red}{A}F_k + 1{-}\delta]}$ \quad\textit{``1 more $k$ $\to$ [MPK $+ 1{-}\delta$] resources, each worth $u_c$.''} \\[3pt]
\textit{\# ECs $=$ \# endogenous states (1 here; 2 in time-to-build).} \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 4 --- Lead EC forward} \\
\hline
Evaluate EC at tomorrow's state: \\[3pt]
$V_k(k', \textcolor{red}{A', s'}) = u_c(c',\textcolor{blue}{n'}) \cdot [\textcolor{red}{A'}F_k(k',\textcolor{blue}{n'}) + 1{-}\delta]$ \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 5 --- Plug into FOC from Step 2 $\to$ Euler} \\
\hline
Replace $V_k(k',\textcolor{red}{A',s'})$ in the $[k']$ FOC: \\[3pt]
$u_c = \beta\,\textcolor{red}{\mathbb{E}}\!\big\{u_c(c',\textcolor{blue}{n'})\,[\textcolor{red}{A'}F_k(k',\textcolor{blue}{n'}) + 1{-}\delta]\big\}$ \\[3pt]
$\boxed{u_c(c,\textcolor{blue}{n}) = \beta\,\textcolor{red}{\mathbb{E}}\!\Big\{u_c(c',\textcolor{blue}{n'})\,\big[\textcolor{red}{A'}F_k(k',\textcolor{blue}{n'}) + 1{-}\delta\big]\Big\}}$ \\[3pt]
\textbf{Euler.} Cost: give up 1 unit of $c$ today ($u_c$). Benefit: $k'$ yields [MPK$' + 1{-}\delta$] $\times u_c' \times \beta$. \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
}

nodes.title: Example: Time-to-Build (2 States, 3-Period Euler)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Time-to-Build: Envelope with 2 Endogenous States}}

Investments made at $t$ become productive only at $t+2$:
\[
\max_{\{c_t, k_{t+1}\}} \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \beta^t \frac{c_t^{1-\sigma}}{1-\sigma}
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad
\begin{cases}
c_t + k_{t+1} = k_{t-1}^{\alpha} + (1-\delta)k_t \\
c_t, k_{t+1} \ge 0, \quad k_{-1}, k_0 \text{ given}
\end{cases}
\]
Production uses $k_{t-1}$, not $k_t$ --- time-to-build.

\medskip
{\footnotesize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.6}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.94\textwidth}@{}}
\hline
\textbf{Step 0 --- States and controls} \\
\hline
\textbf{Endog.\ states:} $k_t$, $k_{t-1}$. \textbf{Control:} $k_{t+1}$ (not $c_t$: substituted out in Step 1). \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 1 --- Substitute $c_t$ out, define $\Phi$} \\
\hline
$\Phi(k_t, k_{t-1}, k_{t+1}) = u(k_{t-1}^{\alpha} + (1{-}\delta)k_t - k_{t+1}) + \beta V(k_{t+1}, k_t)$ \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 2 --- FOC w.r.t.\ control $k_{t+1}$} \\
\hline
$[k_{t+1}]$: $u'(c_t) = \beta\,V_{k}(k_{t+1}, k_t)$ \quad\textit{($V_k$ abstract --- need Steps 3--4)} \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 3 --- Envelope w.r.t.\ each endogenous state (\# ECs $= 2$)} \\
\hline
\textbf{EC-1, w.r.t.\ $k_t$:} enters $c_t$ via $(1{-}\delta)k_t$ AND $\beta V$ as 2nd arg: \\[3pt]
$V_{k_t}(k_t, k_{t-1}) = u'(c_t)(1{-}\delta) + \beta\,V_{k_t}(k_{t+1}, k_t)$ \\[6pt]
\textbf{EC-2, w.r.t.\ $k_{t-1}$:} enters $c_t$ via $k_{t-1}^{\alpha}$ only: \\[3pt]
$V_{k_{t-1}}(k_t, k_{t-1}) = u'(c_t)\cdot\alpha k_{t-1}^{\alpha-1}$ \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 4 --- Lead forward} \\
\hline
Lead EC-1 to $t{+}1$: $V_{k}(k_{t+1}, k_t) = u'(c_{t+1})(1{-}\delta) + \beta\underbrace{V_{k}(k_{t+2}, k_{t+1})}_{\text{still unknown!}}$ \\[6pt]
Lead EC-2 to $t{+}2$ to kill the unknown: $V_{k}(k_{t+2}, k_{t+1}) = u'(c_{t+2})\cdot\alpha k_{t+1}^{\alpha-1}$ \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 5 --- Plug into FOC from Step 2 $\to$ Euler} \\
\hline
$u'(c_t) = \beta[u'(c_{t+1})(1{-}\delta) + \beta\,u'(c_{t+2})\alpha k_{t+1}^{\alpha-1}]$ \\[3pt]
$\boxed{u'(c_t) = \beta u'(c_{t+1})(1{-}\delta) + \beta^2 u'(c_{t+2})\alpha k_{t+1}^{\alpha-1}}$ \\[3pt]
\textbf{3-period Euler}: $c_t \leftrightarrow c_{t+1} \leftrightarrow c_{t+2}$. \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
}

\medskip
\textbf{Why 3 periods?} Investing 1 unit today gives \textbf{two} benefits: (i) $\beta u'(c_{t+1})(1{-}\delta)$: undepreciated capital at $t{+}1$ --- present but not yet productive. (ii) $\beta^2 u'(c_{t+2})\alpha k_{t+1}^{\alpha-1}$: becomes productive at $t{+}2$ --- extra $\beta$ for the delay. If $\delta = 1$: only (ii) survives.

\textbf{Key lesson:} \# envelope conditions $=$ \# endogenous states. With 2 states, you need 2 ECs and may need to lead them forward different numbers of periods to eliminate all abstract $V$ derivatives.

2.1.14 RBC — CE (Recursive): Euler via Envelope Theorem
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{CE (Recursive): Euler via Envelope Theorem}}

Same 5-step algorithm. Only difference: prices $(r^k, w)$ instead of marginal products.

\medskip
{\footnotesize
\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.6}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.94\textwidth}@{}}
\hline
\textbf{Step 0 --- States and controls} \\
\hline
\textbf{States:} $k$ (endogenous), $K, A$ (exogenous to HH). \textbf{Controls:} $\textcolor{blue}{n}, k'$ (not $c$). \\[3pt]
HH takes $r^k(K,A)$, $w(K,A)$, $K' = H(K,A)$ as given. \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 1 --- Substitute $c$ out, define $\Phi$} \\
\hline
$c = (r^k{+}1{-}\delta)k + w\textcolor{blue}{n} - k'$: \\[3pt]
$\Phi(k,\textcolor{blue}{n},k') = u\!\big((r^k{+}1{-}\delta)k + w\textcolor{blue}{n} - k',\;\textcolor{blue}{n}\big) + \beta\,\mathbb{E}[V(k', K', A') \mid A]$ \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 2 --- FOC w.r.t.\ each control} \\
\hline
\textbf{$[\textcolor{blue}{n}]$:} $u_c \cdot w + u_n = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{-u_n = u_c \cdot w}$ \quad\textit{(intratemporal)} \\[6pt]
\textbf{$[k']$:} $-u_c + \beta\,\mathbb{E}[V_k(k', K', A') \mid A] = 0$ \quad\textit{($V_k$ abstract --- need Steps 3--4)} \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 3 --- Envelope w.r.t.\ $k$} \\
\hline
Control terms vanish. $k$ enters budget as $(r^k + 1{-}\delta)k$: \\[3pt]
$\boxed{V_k(k, K, A) = u_c \cdot (r^k + 1{-}\delta)}$ \quad\textit{(HH reads return from price $r^k$, not $AF_k$)} \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 4 --- Lead EC forward} \\
\hline
$V_k(k', K', A') = u_c(c',\textcolor{blue}{n'})\,(r^{k\prime} + 1{-}\delta)$ \\
\hline

\textbf{Step 5 --- Plug into FOC from Step 2 $\to$ Euler} \\
\hline
$\boxed{u_c(c,\textcolor{blue}{n}) = \beta\,\mathbb{E}\!\Big\{u_c(c',\textcolor{blue}{n'})\,(r^k_{t+1} + 1{-}\delta)\Big\}}$ \\[3pt]
\textbf{Euler.} Cost: $u_c$ today. Benefit: market return $r^k_{t+1} + 1{-}\delta$ times $\beta u_c'$. \\[3pt]
\textbf{Equivalence:} Firm FOCs $r^k = AF_k$, $w = AF_n$ $\Rightarrow$ identical to planner Euler (1st Welfare Thm). \\
\hline
\end{tabular}
}

nodes.title: Elasticities
2.1.16 RBC — CE: Technology Shocks & Intertemporal Prices
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textbf{1.} What does a technology shock do?}

Production:
\[
Y_t = A_t F(K_t, N_t)
\]

If $A_t$ increases:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Output rises.
    \item The marginal product of labor rises.
    \item The marginal product of capital rises.
\end{itemize}

In competitive equilibrium:
\[
w_t = A_t F_n(K_t, N_t)
\]
\[
r_t = A_t F_k(K_t, N_t)
\]

Technology directly changes wages and returns.

\vspace{1em}

\textbf{\textbf{2.} Why are these ``intertemporal relative prices''?}

There are two key prices in this model:

\begin{itemize}
    \item[(i)] The wage $w_t$: price of leisure today.
    \item[(ii)] The return $r_{t+1}$: price of consumption tomorrow relative to today.
\end{itemize}

The Euler equation:
\[
u_c(c_t, n_t) = \beta\,\mathbb{E}_t\{u_c(c_{t+1}, n_{t+1})\,[r^k_{t+1} + 1-\delta]\}
\]

implies:
\[
r_{t+1}
=
\text{price of future consumption in units of today's consumption.}
\]

So:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Wage = intratemporal relative price (leisure vs.\ consumption today).
    \item Return = intertemporal relative price (today vs.\ tomorrow consumption).
\end{itemize}

\vspace{1em}

\textbf{\textbf{3.} What happens after a positive technology shock?}

Suppose $A_t$ increases temporarily.

Then:
\[
w_t \uparrow
\]
\[
r_t \uparrow
\]

This changes:
\begin{itemize}
    \item The price of leisure today (higher wage $\Rightarrow$ leisure more expensive).
    \item The price of consuming tomorrow (higher return $\Rightarrow$ future consumption more attractive).
\end{itemize}

Households therefore face new relative prices across time.

nodes.title: 2.1.17 RBC — Critiques & Limitations
2.1.18 S&M: Motivation & Key Modeling Choices
S&M: Worker Flows vs Job Flows
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Worker Flows vs Job Flows}}

\textbf{Worker flows} (measured by JOLTS): hires and separations at the individual level, including job-to-job transitions, entries into unemployment, and exits from the labour force.

\textbf{Job flows} (measured by BED data): establishment-level employment changes. An ``establishment'' = a single physical workplace (factory, store, office). Count workers this quarter vs last: if headcount rose $\Rightarrow$ \emph{job creation}; if it fell $\Rightarrow$ \emph{job destruction}. Internal replacements are invisible.

\textbf{Accounting relationship.} Some separations are replaced without affecting job destruction; some hires replace departing workers without contributing to job creation:
\[
\text{Hires} > \text{Job creation}, \qquad \text{Separations} > \text{Job destruction}
\]
The gap is churning/replacement within establishments.

\textbf{Cyclical patterns:}
\begin{itemize}[nosep]
    \item \textbf{Quits} (major driver of hires): \emph{procyclical} --- workers switch jobs more in tight markets.
    \item \textbf{Layoffs} (tied to job destruction): \emph{countercyclical} --- recessions trigger contractions.
    \item Job creation stabilises faster in recovery; hires swing more due to the cyclical quit component.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Relevance for S\&M models:} S\&M focuses on \emph{worker} flows (individual transitions between employment and unemployment), not job flows. The matching function captures the hiring process; the separation rate $\lambda$ captures job loss.

2.1.2 RBC — Preferences: Utility Specification
nodes.content:
\textbf{Utility}
\begin{itemize}
    \item A common parametric specification for utility:
    
    \[
    u(c_t, n_t) = \frac{c_t^{1-\sigma} - 1}{1 - \sigma} - \frac{n_t^{1+\varphi}}{1 + \varphi}
    \quad \text{for } \sigma \neq 1
    \]
    
    \[
    u(c_t, n_t) = \log c_t - \frac{n_t^{1+\varphi}}{1 + \varphi}
    \quad \text{as } \sigma \to 1
    \]
    
    \item $\sigma$: curvature of utility (inverse of IES for consumption). \item $\varphi$: curvature of labor disutility ($1/\varphi$ = Frisch elasticity).

\end{itemize}\\\\





\bigskip
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Why $\sigma \to 1$ gives log utility (L'H\^opital)}}

\[
\lim_{\sigma\to 1} \frac{c^{1-\sigma} - 1}{1-\sigma} = \;\text{``}\tfrac{0}{0}\text{''} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \text{L'H\^opital w.r.t.\ } \sigma
\]
\textbf{Trick:} rewrite $c^{1-\sigma} = e^{(1-\sigma)\ln c}$ so you can differentiate w.r.t.\ $\sigma$:
\[
\frac{d}{d\sigma}\!\big(e^{(1-\sigma)\ln c} - 1\big) = -\ln c \cdot e^{(1-\sigma)\ln c}, \qquad \frac{d}{d\sigma}(1-\sigma) = -1
\]
\[
\Rightarrow\quad \lim_{\sigma\to 1} \frac{-\ln c \cdot e^{(1-\sigma)\ln c}}{-1} = \ln c \cdot e^{0} = \boxed{\ln c}
\]

\textbf{Production}:\\
 $F(k_t, n_t) = k_t^{\alpha} n_t^{1-\alpha}$ (Cobb-Douglas, CRS).

nodes.title: 2.1.5 RBC — Planner (Sequential): Lagrangian, FOCs & Boundary Conditions
2.1.10 RBC — CE (Sequential): Lagrangian, FOCs & Boundary Conditions
2.1.11 RBC — CE: Equilibrium Definition
Guess and Verify Solution Method
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Guess and Verify ($\sigma = 1$, $\delta = 1$)}}

With $\sigma = 1$: $u(c) = \ln c$. With $\delta = 1$: full depreciation, so $k_{t+1} = k_t^{\alpha} - c_t$.

\textbf{Euler equation} becomes: $1/c_t = \beta\,\alpha k_{t+1}^{\alpha-1}/c_{t+1}$.

\textbf{Guess:} $c_t = A\,k_t^{\alpha}$ and $k_{t+1} = B\,k_t^{\alpha}$, with $A + B = 1$ (from RC: $c_t + k_{t+1} = k_t^{\alpha}$).

\textbf{Verify:} plug into Euler:
\[
\frac{1}{A\,k_t^{\alpha}} = \frac{\beta\,\alpha(B\,k_t^{\alpha})^{\alpha-1}}{A\,(B\,k_t^{\alpha})^{\alpha}}
= \frac{\beta\,\alpha}{A\,B\,k_t^{\alpha}}
\]
Cancel $1/(A\,k_t^{\alpha})$:
\[
1 = \frac{\beta\alpha}{B} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{B = \alpha\beta}, \qquad \boxed{A = 1 - \alpha\beta}
\]

\textbf{Policy functions:}
\[
\boxed{c_t = (1-\alpha\beta)\,k_t^{\alpha}, \qquad k_{t+1} = \alpha\beta\,k_t^{\alpha}}
\]
The household saves a constant fraction $\alpha\beta$ of output and consumes the rest. This is an \textbf{exact} solution (no approximation), but only works under $\sigma = 1$, $\delta = 1$.

\bigskip
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Policy functions and MIT shocks.}}

With policy functions $c_t = (1-\alpha\beta)k_t^{\alpha}$ and $k_{t+1} = \alpha\beta\,k_t^{\alpha}$:

\textbf{Case 1: No shock.} The planner follows the policy functions. In period $t=1$, it is still optimal to choose $c_1 = f(k_1)$ and $k_2 = g(k_1)$. This follows from the optimality principle.

\textbf{Case 2: MIT shock ($k_1 \neq g(k_0)$).} The planner still follows the policy functions but at the \emph{new} state: $c_1 = f(k_1)$ and $k_2 = g(k_1)$. The problem's structure (preferences, technology, $\delta, \beta, \alpha$) is unchanged --- only the state has shifted. The policy functions map \emph{any} realization of the state into optimal controls.

\textbf{This is the fundamental advantage of the recursive formulation over the sequential one.} The sequential approach gives a pre-computed list of date-indexed actions; if $k_1 \neq k_1^*$, the planner must re-solve from scratch. The recursive approach delivers policy functions that work for any state --- no re-optimization needed.

nodes.title: Solution Methods
RBC — Indivisible Labor (Rogerson 1988, Hansen 1985)
nodes.content:
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{The Problem: Extensive Margin}}

In standard RBC, labor supply varies along the \textcolor{red}{intensive margin} (how many hours). Rogerson (1988) and Hansen (1985) study the \textcolor{red}{extensive margin}: work $\bar{n}$ hours or not at all. $n \in \{0, \bar{n}\}$ --- the choice set is \textbf{non-convex}.

\medskip
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Rogerson (1988): Static Model}}

Production: $y = zn$, competitive $\Rightarrow$ $w = z$ (wage is marginal productivity). Preferences: $u(c) - v(n)$, separable, with $u'>0$, $u''<0$, $v'>0$, $v''\ge 0$. 

\medskip
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Employment Lotteries (Convexification)}}

Each household chooses a \textcolor{red}{probability of working} $\alpha \in [0,1]$:
\begin{itemize}
    \item With probability $\alpha$: work $\bar{n}$. With probability $1-\alpha$: not work.
    \item \textcolor{red}{Full insurance}: consumption identical across employment states. HH paid by expected hours $\alpha\bar{n}$.
    \item Identical HH choose same $\alpha$, so \textcolor{red}{aggregate labor} $n = \alpha\bar{n}$.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Optimization:}
\[
\max_{c, \alpha} \; u(c) - [\alpha\, v(\bar{n}) + (1-\alpha)\,v(0)] \quad \text{s.t.} \quad c = \alpha z\bar{n}
\]
FOCs (two controls: $c$ and $\alpha$):
\begin{itemize}
    \item w.r.t.\ $c$: $u'(c) = \lambda$
    \item w.r.t.\ $\alpha$: differentiate the expected disutility $-[\alpha v(\bar{n}) + (1-\alpha)v(0)]$ to get $-[v(\bar{n}) - v(0)]$. The budget gives $+\lambda z\bar{n}$. Setting to zero:
\end{itemize}
\[
v(\bar{n}) - v(0) = \lambda z\bar{n}
\]
The LHS is the marginal cost of raising $\alpha$ (employment probability): you become slightly more likely to work $\bar{n}$ hours, so you pay the disutility gap $v(\bar{n}) - v(0)$. The RHS is the marginal benefit: slightly more likely to earn wage $z\bar{n}$, worth $\lambda$ per unit.

Substitute $\lambda = u'(c)$:
\[
\boxed{v(\bar{n}) - v(0) = u'(c)\, z\bar{n}}
\]

\medskip
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Key Result: Linear Disutility at Aggregate Level}}

Normalize $v(0) = 0$. Expected utility $= u(c) - \alpha v(\bar{n})$. Since $n = \alpha\bar{n}$:
\[
u(c) - \frac{v(\bar{n})}{\bar{n}}\, n = u(c) - \gamma n, \qquad \gamma \equiv \frac{v(\bar{n})}{\bar{n}}.
\]
\textcolor{red}{Utility is linear in labor} $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{implied Frisch elasticity is infinite} ($\varphi = 0$ in $n^{1+\varphi}/(1+\varphi)$).

\medskip
\textbf{\textcolor{blue}{Hansen (1985): Dynamic RBC with Indivisible Labor}}

Embed in RBC: each period HH chooses $\alpha_t \in [0,1]$, $n_t = \alpha_t\bar{n}$, with full insurance.
\[
\max_{\{c_t, \alpha_t, k_{t+1}\}} \mathbb{E}_0 \sum_{t=0}^{\infty} \beta^t [u(c_t) - \alpha_t v(\bar{n})]
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad c_t + k_{t+1} \le (r_t + 1-\delta)k_t + w_t\alpha_t\bar{n}
\]

Using $n_t = \alpha_t\bar{n}$ and $\gamma = v(\bar{n})/\bar{n}$, this becomes:
\[
\max \mathbb{E}_0 \sum \beta^t [u(c_t) - \gamma n_t]
\quad \text{s.t.} \quad c_t + k_{t+1} \le (r_t + 1-\delta)k_t + w_t n_t
\]

\textbf{Why is this $\varphi = 0$?} We don't need to know the functional form of $v$. All that matters: $v(\bar{n})$ is a constant (the disutility of working the fixed shift $\bar{n}$), $\bar{n}$ is a constant, so $\gamma = v(\bar{n})/\bar{n}$ is just a positive constant. The disutility term is $\gamma n_t$ --- linear in $n_t$. Now compare with the standard RBC disutility $\gamma \cdot n_t^{1+\varphi}/(1+\varphi)$: when $\varphi = 0$, this is $\gamma \cdot n_t^1/1 = \gamma n_t$. Same thing. The value of $\gamma$ gets calibrated anyway (normalization), so the specific form of $v$ is irrelevant --- only the linearity matters.

Same Bellman, same FOCs, same Euler. Only difference: \textbf{labor disutility is linear} ($\varphi = 0$, infinite Frisch elasticity). This generates much larger labor supply responses to shocks, helping RBC match the volatility of hours.

trash.title: Uncertainty: Time-Invariant Markov Chains
trash.content:
\begin{itemize}
    \item Assume $s_t$ follows a discrete-time, finite-state, time-invariant Markov chain.
    
    \begin{itemize}
        \item \textcolor{red}{Markov property}: the next state depends only on the current state, not on the full past history.
        
        \item \textcolor{red}{Time invariance}: transition probabilities do not depend on time.
    \end{itemize}
\end{itemize}

\[
\pi(s^{t+1} \mid s^t)
=
\pi(s^{t+1} \mid s_t, s_{t-1}, \ldots, s_0)
=
\pi(s^{t+1} \mid s_t).
\]

\bigskip

\begin{itemize}
    \item The Markov property implies:
\end{itemize}

\[
\pi(s^t)
=
\pi(s_t \mid s_{t-1})
\pi(s_{t-1} \mid s_{t-2})
\cdots
\pi(s_1 \mid s_0)
\pi_0(s_0),
\]

\[
\pi(s^t \mid s^\tau)
=
\pi(s_t \mid s_{t-1})
\pi(s_{t-1} \mid s_{t-2})
\cdots
\pi(s_{\tau+1} \mid s_\tau).
\]

trash.title: Uncertainty: Markov Technology Process
trash.content:
\section*{Technology Process Governed by a Markov Process}

\begin{itemize}
    \item Let the aggregate technology level $A_t(s^t)$ be a time-invariant function of last period’s level and the current shock $s_t$:
    
    \[
    A_t(s^t) = A\!\big(A_{t-1}(s^{t-1}),\, s_t\big).
    \]
    
    This means productivity evolves recursively: current productivity depends only on last period’s productivity and the current shock. The entire past history matters only through $A_{t-1}$ (Markov property).
    
   
    \item In recursive notation:
    
    \[
    A' = A s,
    \]
    
    where $A$ denotes current (past) productivity and $A'$ next period productivity. This compact form highlights the Markov structure: given $A$, only the current shock $s$ is needed to determine $A'$.
\end{itemize}
